summary:
Visitors in Moscow stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 prohibits legal gender recognition outright: it bans gender-affirming surgery, removes any route to changing a gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex". The provisions reach speech that justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, entered on the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

Moscow is where the designation has been applied most directly. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in the city; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Kotov, the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024. In the same month, a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025.

Proceedings have produced custodial terms. Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation was reported in February 2025 and concerned organising, on the basis of a court ruling in Siberia reported in January 2025.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally.

Entry and onward-protection context carries an explicit warning for LGBT travellers. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting published in June 2024 profiles Russians caught in limbo between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes the court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians; for many transgender Russians emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, and escaped only after police responded to a phone she had found.

A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule that bears directly on foreign visitors and on what their presence in the country signals to authorities.

The UK Home Office standard, which treats LGBT+ people in Russia as a particular social group under the refugee convention, sets the assessment for UK asylum claims and is the benchmark a visitor fleeing persecution would be measured against.
localsOnly:
Residents diagnosed with gender dysphoria lose the right to adopt, and any marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex is void under the 2023 law. No administrative route to a changed gender marker remains.

There is no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, no hate-crime designation, and no aggravating-factor treatment of gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation in sentencing; the state does not record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community.

Community organisations have been removed by court order: nine LGBTQ bodies, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist between March and May 2026.

The Moscow Registry Office has refused same-sex marriages publicly since at least 2011, when its head stated that attempts by same-sex couples to marry in Moscow are "doomed to fail", and the city has never approved a gay pride rally.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory states what penalty regime applies to a foreign national detained in Moscow under the extremist or propaganda provisions, or whether consular screening at entry flags gender markers that no longer match Russian documents; that question is unresolved here.

Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation was handed down on the basis of a court ruling in Siberia, and the inventory records no Moscow-specific custodial outcomes; whether Moscow courts have issued comparable sentences is not sourced.

Whether the November 2023 extremist designation has been challenged on appeal, and the current status of any such proceeding, is not sourced in this inventory.

The February 2025 prison-sentence report and the June 2025 Human Rights Watch count predate the March to May 2026 extremist listings of nine organisations, so the two datasets are not on a common timeline.
